---
title: "Filtering data by attribute"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 6,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

[Filtering by area](filtering-by-area.html) answers *"give me this layer, but
only within that area"*. This article is about the other kind of question:
*"give me only the features **with these properties**"* — the addresses with
one postal code, the streets whose name starts with "Lange", the thousands of
buildings whose id appears in your own data. Attribute filters run **on the
PDOK server**, so only the matching features are downloaded — often the
difference between transferring a few rows and a few hundred thousand.

Server-side filtering follows the OGC
[CQL2](https://www.ogc.org/standards/cql2/) standard, which PDOK offers on
every dataset with an OGC API Features service. It was introduced on the BAG
first (announced [on the PDOK
Geoforum](https://geoforum.nl/t/bag-ogc-api-uitgebreid-met-nieuwe-filterfunctionaliteit-demo-beschikbaar/11778))
and has since been enabled across the platform. The server rejects a filter
it cannot handle with a clear error — it never silently returns unfiltered
data.

```{r setup}
library(pdokr)
library(tmap)
```

## Which fields can you filter on?

Each layer publishes its *queryables*: the fields a server-side filter may
reference. `pdok_list_queryables()` retrieves them for one layer;
`pdok_list_layers(dataset, queryables = TRUE)` adds them as a column for
every layer of a dataset at once.

```{r queryables}
pdok_list_queryables("kadaster/bag", "adres")
```

The queryables are chosen per layer and are often a small subset of the
layer's attributes. The generalized municipalities of CBS, for example, can
be filtered on the year but not on the municipality name:

```{r queryables-cbs}
pdok_list_queryables("cbs/gebiedsindelingen", "gemeente_gegeneraliseerd")
```

A filter on any other field is rejected, with the server's explanation and a
pointer back to the queryables:

```{r queryables-error, error = TRUE}
pdok_read(
  "cbs/gebiedsindelingen", "gemeente_gegeneraliseerd",
  filter = pdok_where(statnaam == "Utrecht")
)
```

So check the queryables first. For a field that is not queryable, load the
layer (within an area, if it is large) and subset the `sf` in R as usual.

## Filter with R syntax: `pdok_where()`

`pdok_where()` translates a familiar R expression into the CQL2 filter
language for you. Field names are written as bare names; values come from
your R session, so variables and vectors work as usual.

```{r where-simple}
pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "adres",
  filter = pdok_where(postcode == "3811MZ")
)
```

The same works on every dataset. The CBS neighbourhoods, for instance, are
queryable by municipality name, which fetches exactly one municipality's
neighbourhoods without any spatial filtering:

```{r where-cbs}
buurten <- pdok_read(
  "cbs/wijken-en-buurten-2025", "buurten",
  filter = pdok_where(gemeentenaam == "Amersfoort")
)
nrow(buurten)
```

Conditions combine with `&`, `|` and `!`, and `%in%` matches against a
vector:

```{r where-combine}
codes <- c("3811MZ", "3811MS")

addresses <- pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "adres",
  filter = pdok_where(postcode %in% codes & huisnummer != "1")
)
nrow(addresses)
```

`like()` matches string patterns (`%` is the wildcard), and `casei()` makes a
comparison case-insensitive:

```{r where-like}
lange <- pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "adres",
  filter = pdok_where(
    casei(woonplaats_naam) == "amersfoort" &
      like(openbare_ruimte_naam, "Lange%")
  )
)
sort(unique(lange$openbare_ruimte_naam))
```

```{r map-interactive}
tmap_mode("view")

tm_basemap(pdok_basemap("grijs")) +
  tm_shape(lange) +
  tm_dots(fill = "openbare_ruimte_naam", size = 0.5, id = "openbare_ruimte_naam",
          fill.legend = tm_legend("Street")) +
  tm_credits("Kaartgegevens © Kadaster")
```

```{r reset, include = FALSE}
tmap_mode("plot")
```

The full translation table — including `between()`, `is.na()` and the
accent-insensitive `accenti()` — is in `?pdok_where`. A `pdok_where` object
prints the CQL2 it stands for, which is a handy way to learn the language:

```{r where-print}
pdok_where(casei(woonplaats_naam) == "amersfoort" & huisnummer >= 10)
```

## Combining with an area filter

An attribute filter and a spatial filter answer different halves of one
question, and they work together in a single call: the server applies the
attribute filter (and the bounding box), and `pdok_read()` then clips the
result to the exact shape.

Without the attribute filter this would download every address in the
municipality's bounding box — hundreds of thousands of features. With it, the
server sends only the "Lange…" addresses, and the exact clip to the boundary
happens locally as usual.

```{r combine-area}
amersfoort <- pdok_geocode("Amersfoort", type = "gemeente")

pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "adres",
  filter_by = amersfoort, # spatial: within this boundary
  filter = pdok_where(like(openbare_ruimte_naam, "Lange%")) # attribute: on the server
) |>
  nrow()
```

## Which values can a field take?

The queryables tell you which fields exist, not which values they hold. For
the BAG the authoritative source is the official [Catalogus
BAG](https://imbag.github.io/catalogus/), whose [domain values
chapter](https://imbag.github.io/catalogus/hoofdstukken/domeinwaarden) defines
the permitted values — for `gebruiksdoel`, for example, the eleven fixed uses
(`woonfunctie`, `onderwijsfunctie`, `winkelfunctie`, ...). Other datasets have
their own documentation.

You can also just look at the data: read a modest sample and inspect the
column.

```{r values}
buildings <- pdok_read("kadaster/bag", "pand", bbox = amersfoort, max_features = 500)
sort(unique(unlist(strsplit(buildings$gebruiksdoel, ","))))
```

The `strsplit()` is there because of a BAG subtlety that matters for
filtering, covered next.

## Multi-value fields: `has()`

As the sample shows, `gebruiksdoel` often holds *several* comma-joined
values: a building inherits the use of every unit in it, so a school with a
gym and a caretaker's flat is registered as, say,
`"onderwijsfunctie,sportfunctie,woonfunctie"`. An equality test only matches
buildings whose *entire* value is `"onderwijsfunctie"` and silently misses
the rest. `has()` expresses what you usually mean — *the field contains this
value*:

```{r has}
schools <- pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "pand",
  filter_by = amersfoort,
  filter = pdok_where(has(gebruiksdoel, "onderwijsfunctie"))
)
nrow(schools)

# with == instead of has() we would have missed the combined-use buildings:
nrow(pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "pand",
  filter_by = amersfoort,
  filter = pdok_where(gebruiksdoel == "onderwijsfunctie")
))
```

## Thousands of ids at once

A common pattern is a table from another source that carries BAG ids — for
example DUO's school locations, which have a `BAG_ID` column (see [Combining
with external data](duo-schools.html)). With `%in%` you can fetch exactly
those features, whatever their number: PDOK limits how long a request URL may
be, so `pdok_where()` automatically spreads a long value list over multiple
requests (300 values each) and `pdok_read()` combines the results.

```{r batching}
# Stand-in for ids from your own data: 700 addresses around the center
ids <- pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "adres",
  filter = pdok_where(like(postcode, "3811%")),
  max_features = 700
)$identificatie

# 700 ids -> three requests behind the scenes, one sf back
mine <- pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "adres",
  filter = pdok_where(identificatie %in% ids)
)
nrow(mine)
```

Row order follows the service, not your id vector, so join on the id column
rather than relying on position.

## Writing CQL2 yourself

`pdok_where()` covers the common cases, but `filter` also accepts a raw CQL2
text string, passed to the server unchanged — useful for CQL2 features the
translation does not expose.

```{r raw-cql}
wijersstraat <- pdok_read(
  "kadaster/bag", "adres",
  filter = "postcode = '3811MZ' AND huisnummer = '1'"
)
paste(wijersstraat$openbare_ruimte_naam, wijersstraat$huisnummer)
```

A quick tour of the language (the [CQL2
standard](https://docs.ogc.org/is/21-065r2/21-065r2.html) has the full
grammar):

| CQL2 | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `postcode = '3811MZ'`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | comparisons; strings in single quotes |
| `a AND b`, `a OR b`, `NOT (a)` | logic (AND binds tighter than OR) |
| `postcode IN ('3811MZ', '3811MS')` | value lists |
| `openbare_ruimte_naam LIKE 'Lange%'` | patterns; `%` = any characters |
| `huisnummer BETWEEN 1 AND 9` | ranges |
| `casei(...)`, `accenti(...)` | case-/accent-insensitive, applied to both sides |
| `huisletter IS NULL` | missing values |
| `S_INTERSECTS(geometry, POINT(5.387 52.156))` | spatial predicates, coordinates in lon/lat |

Spatial CQL2 functions such as `S_INTERSECTS` work, with two things to know.
First, always combine them with a `bbox`: without one the server tests the
geometry against the whole country and a single point takes 15 seconds,
while with a bounding box the same request answers in about a second.
Second, the server's cost grows with the number of points *and* the size of
the box, so this is a tool for a neighbourhood or a city, not a province.
For polygons the plain `filter_by` is faster than a server-side
`S_INTERSECTS`, and for a small set of points `pdok_read()` already adds the
spatial filter for you (see the `filter_by` argument), so writing
`S_INTERSECTS` by hand is rarely needed.

The server validates every filter and pdokr passes its explanation on, so a
mistake is easy to diagnose:

```{r raw-error, error = TRUE}
pdok_read("kadaster/bag", "adres", filter = "postcode == '3811MZ'")
```
